data.title: Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura (RAPK)?**
- Rare autosomal dominant disorder (ADAM10 loss-of-function) of slightly depressed, angulated, reticulate brown freckle-like macules on the dorsa of hands and feet, starting in childhood/adolescence and slowly spreading proximally; worse with sun exposure
- Palmar and plantar pits (breaks in dermatoglyphics) — characteristic

**Q2. Histopathology.**
- Epidermal atrophy with thin elongated rete ridges, increased basal pigmentation and melanocytes at the tips of rete — atrophic lentigo-like pattern

**Q3. Differential diagnosis.**
- Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (hypo + hyperpigmented mottling on dorsa, Japanese — ADAR1)
- Dowling–Degos disease (flexural; overlap cases exist)
- Acropigmentation of Dohi, freckles, lentigines, Peutz–Jeghers, Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn, dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis, acral pigmentation of B12 deficiency, Addison's

**Q4. Enumerate reticulate pigmentary disorders.**
- Dowling–Degos disease (flexural reticulate pigmentation, comedo-like pits — KRT5, POFUT1, POGLUT1)
- Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura (dorsa of hands/feet, palmar pits — ADAM10)
- Galli–Galli disease (DDD with acantholysis)
- Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (Dohi — acral mottled hypo/hyper — ADAR1) and dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria
- Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn syndrome and dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis (KRT14 — absent dermatoglyphics)
- Dyskeratosis congenita (reticulate pigmentation, nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia — telomere genes)
- Incontinentia pigmenti stage 3, X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder, Haber syndrome, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (acquired)

**Q5. Treatment.**
- No definitive therapy; photoprotection; topical azelaic acid/hydroquinone or adapalene; Q-switched/Er:YAG laser (case reports); genetic counselling

**Q6. What is the pathogenesis?**
- ADAM10 (a disintegrin and metalloprotease 10) loss-of-function → impaired Notch signalling in skin, affecting melanocyte homeostasis and epidermal differentiation

**Q7. Clinical clues helping diagnosis.**
- Onset first/second decade, autosomal dominant family history, freckle-like angulated macules that are slightly atrophic/depressed, on dorsa of hands and feet, gradually extending to forearms, neck and face; palmar pits and interruptions of dermatoglyphics; darkens with sun

**Q8. How does dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria differ?**
- DSH (Dohi): both hyper- and hypopigmented small macules (mottled) on dorsa of hands and feet, ADAR1 mutation, East Asians, no palmar pits; RAPK: only hyperpigmented atrophic angulated macules with palmar pits

**Q9. Is there any malignant association?**
- No — benign cosmetic disorder; overlap with Dowling–Degos disease (shared features in some families) is recognised

**Q10. Dermoscopy of RAPK.**
- Brown reticular pigment network with irregular brown dots/ globules on dorsa of hands; palmar pits seen as small depressions interrupting dermatoglyphics

**Q11. Explain the significance of palmar pits as a sign — other causes.**
- Palmar pits: RAPK, basal cell naevus (Gorlin) syndrome, Darier's disease (punctate keratoses/ pits), Cowden syndrome (acral keratoses), punctate palmoplantar keratoderma, arsenical keratoses, pitted keratolysis (soles)

**Q12. What are the dyschromatoses?**
- Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (DSH — ADAR1, acral mixed hyper/hypopigmented macules from childhood, Japanese/Chinese) and dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (ABCB6/SASH1 — generalised mottling); RAPK is hyperpigmentation only

**Q13. Explain the role of photoprotection.**
- Lesions darken with sun exposure; sunscreens and gloves reduce contrast; pigment otherwise stable and benign

**Q14. Differentiate RAPK from acral pigmentation in vitamin B12 deficiency.**
- B12 deficiency: diffuse hyperpigmentation of knuckles, palms, soles and nails (vegetarians, pernicious anaemia), with anaemia, glossitis, neuropathy — reversible with B12; RAPK is reticulate, genetic, with palmar pits

**Q15. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Angulated reticulate pigmented macules on dorsa of hands with palmar pits — RAPK (ADAM10)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Reticulate pigmentary disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
